questions.question:
D4 — Use the job library's retry hooks with a custom backoff function, or roll the inline scheduler as planned?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md "Add background job retry framework", finding F1 (PLAN.md:6-8).
ELI10: The plan says the job library already has retry hooks but rebuilds a scheduler inside each worker to control the delay curve. A scheduler is more than a curve: it has to store the delayed attempt somewhere that survives a worker restart, avoid double-running when the library's own retry also fires, and be observable. Libraries in this class expose the curve as a plug-in delay function, so you can own the curve without owning the scheduler.
Stakes if we pick wrong: an in-process scheduler that sleeps or sets a timer loses every pending retry on deploy or crash, silently; the user's job just never completes and nothing reports it.
Recommendation: A because it keeps the curve control the plan asks for and drops the part of the plan that duplicates a Layer 1 built-in. [Layer 1]
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: own the curve (A) vs own the curve plus scheduling correctness (B, C).

options.label: Library retry hook + shared backoff fn (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Delayed attempts persist and survive restarts because the library re-enqueues them (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
✅ Curve control via one custom delay function; attempt count, logging, and dispatch come from the library
❌ Curve is bounded by what the hook exposes (attempt number, error); exotic per-job curves need a workaround

options.label: Custom inline scheduler per worker, as planned
options.description:
✅ Total control over timing and dispatch inside each worker
✅ No dependence on library hook semantics or version changes
❌ You own persistence, restart survival, dedup against the library's retry path, and 5 copies of it (human: ~1 week / CC: ~1 hr plus ongoing ownership)

options.label: Custom scheduler as one shared module
options.description:
✅ Full control with a single implementation instead of 5 copies
✅ Easier to test and swap later than inline copies
❌ Still rebuilds persistence and dispatch the library already provides (human: ~3 days / CC: ~40 min)

questions.question:
D5 — When a job keeps failing, what ends the retries and where does the job go?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md retry framework, finding F5 (PLAN.md:6-8); R1 fixed as library hook + shared backoff.
ELI10: The plan defines how long to wait between tries but not when to stop or what happens after. Two things need an answer: some errors will never succeed on retry (a 422 validation error, a 404), so retrying them just burns time; and once retries are exhausted the job needs a place to land where a human sees it. A dead-letter queue is that place, plus an alert so someone actually looks.
Stakes if we pick wrong: exhausted or permanently failing jobs vanish; the user's webhook, email, or export never arrives and no one is paged.
Recommendation: A because a retry loop with no exit or no destination is a silent-failure machine, and the full version is ~15 minutes of CC time.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Net: full observability of failed jobs vs relying on someone remembering to check the failed set.

options.label: Cap + fail-fast on permanent errors + dead-letter with alert (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Permanent errors (4xx except 429, validation) skip retries entirely and land in dead-letter on attempt 1
✅ Exhausted jobs are visible and alert-worthy; nothing is silently dropped (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15 min)
❌ Needs an error-classification function and an alert hook, both of which need tests

options.label: Cap + fail-fast; failed jobs stay in library failed set, no alert
options.description:
✅ No alerting integration to build; the library's failed set already exists
✅ Still stops permanent errors from burning the retry budget (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
❌ Nobody is told; failed jobs are only found by someone opening the dashboard

options.label: Attempt cap only
options.description:
✅ Smallest change: one number on the retry options
✅ Guarantees the loop terminates (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~3 min)
❌ Permanent errors retry N times for nothing, and exhausted jobs are not routed or reported

answers.D5 \u2014 When a job keeps failing, what: Cap + fail-fast on permanent errors + dead-letter with alert (recommended)

questions.question:
D6 — What shape is the backoff curve: jitter and a maximum delay, or raw exponential?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md retry framework, finding F6 (PLAN.md:6-8); R1 and R4 fixed.
ELI10: Exponential backoff doubles the wait each attempt: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s. Two problems with the raw version. First, if 500 jobs fail at the same moment because a downstream API blipped, they all retry at exactly the same moments too, which re-creates the spike. Jitter adds randomness so they spread out. Second, without a ceiling, attempt 8 is minutes away and attempt 12 is hours; a cap (say 5 minutes) keeps the tail sane.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a 30-second outage turns into repeated self-inflicted spikes, and users wait far longer than needed for late attempts.
Recommendation: A because both additions are a few lines in the shared backoff function and they are the two things every source on retry design agrees on.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Net: three-line curve that behaves under load vs the textbook curve that misbehaves in exactly the scenario retries exist for.

options.label: Exponential + full jitter + max delay cap (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Retries after a shared outage spread out instead of arriving in lockstep
✅ Late attempts are bounded (e.g. cap 5 min), so total time-to-dead-letter is predictable (human: ~2 hr / CC: ~5 min)
❌ Jitter makes exact delays non-deterministic; tests must inject the random source

options.label: Exponential + max delay cap, no jitter
options.description:
✅ Deterministic delays, trivially testable
✅ Tail is still bounded by the cap (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~3 min)
❌ Every job that failed together retries together; retry storms remain possible

options.label: Raw exponential
options.description:
✅ Simplest possible function, matches the plan's wording
✅ Nothing to configure beyond the base delay (human: ~30 min / CC: ~2 min)
❌ Lockstep retries and an unbounded tail; attempt 5 at base 1s is 16s but base 5s is 80s and climbing

answers.D6 \u2014 What shape is the backoff curv: Exponential + full jitter + max delay cap (recommended)

The plan copies that block into 5 files and promises to dedupe later. A shared module means each worker gets one line (register the retry policy) and every future fix lands once. Stakes if we pick wrong: 5 places to patch when the classifier misses an error type; one worker inevitably ends up with a stale copy and different retry behavior in production.
Recommendation: A because the shared module costs ~10 minutes of CC time now and the approved handlers have to live somewhere anyway.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=4/10
Net: one source of truth now vs a known debt with a vague due date.

✅ Tested once, at the unit level, instead of 5 sets of near-identical tests (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
❌ Per-worker overrides (different caps) need an options parameter rather than inline edits

questions.question:
D8 — What delivery contract does `processWebhookJob()` keep after the rewrite, and what does its regression test assert?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md retry framework, finding F2 (PLAN.md:16-18); R1, R2, R4, R5 fixed.
ELI10: Today a webhook is sent at most once: if it fails, it fails, but the receiver never gets it twice. Adding retries changes that unless you are careful: a request that times out may have already been processed by the receiver, and retrying it sends a duplicate (a second "order.paid" event). Some failures are safe to retry because the request never left: connection refused, DNS failure, TLS handshake failure. The question is which guarantee receivers get after this change, and the regression test pins that guarantee so a later edit cannot quietly break it.
Stakes if we pick wrong: your customers' systems receive duplicate events with no way to tell, or you lose a guarantee they built on without telling them.
Recommendation: A because it keeps the promise receivers already rely on and still retries the failures that are provably safe. B is the industry-standard long-term shape (Stripe-style idempotency header) but it is an external contract change that needs receiver communication, which is CEO/product scope, not this PR.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: preserve the contract and retry the safe half (A) vs change the contract for full retry (B) vs preserve it with no retry at all (C).

options.label: Preserve at-most-once; retry only pre-send failures (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Receivers never see a duplicate; connect-refused/DNS/TLS failures still get retried with jitter
✅ Regression test: timeout → exactly 1 POST + dead-letter; connect-refused → retried, same body; success path unchanged (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
❌ Timeouts and 5xx after send go to dead-letter for manual action rather than auto-retry

options.label: Move to at-least-once with idempotency key header
options.description:
✅ Full retry on timeouts and 5xx; receivers dedupe on a stable delivery id per event
✅ Regression test: header identical across attempts; duplicates only after a retryable failure (human: ~3 days incl. comms / CC: ~20 min + comms)
❌ External contract change: every receiver must dedupe or they will see duplicate events

options.label: Preserve at-most-once by opting webhooks out of retry
options.description:
✅ Simplest: webhooks skip `registerRetryPolicy`; behavior is exactly today's
✅ Regression test: any failure → exactly 1 POST + dead-letter (human: ~2 hr / CC: ~10 min)
❌ Gains nothing from this change for the job type most likely to hit transient failures

answers.D8 \u2014 What delivery contract does `p: Preserve at-most-once; retry only pre-send failures (recommended)

questions.question:
D9 — Cache the dependency graph across retry attempts, or keep recomputing it and measure first?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md retry framework, finding F4 (PLAN.md:21-23); R1-R5 fixed.
ELI10: Each retry reloads the whole job payload from the database and rebuilds its dependency graph from scratch. The plan notes it could cache the graph after the first attempt but skips it. Caching is only worth it if the recompute is actually slow, and nobody has measured that. Caching also adds a correctness risk: if the payload changes between attempts, a cached graph is stale. Retries are now capped at 5 attempts, so the worst case is bounded.
Stakes if we pick wrong: cache too early and a stale graph produces a wrong result on retry (a correctness bug); never cache and a heavy job's retries add DB load and latency you could have avoided.
Recommendation: B because a slow retry is a latency cost and a stale cache is a correctness bug; add the timing metric now, and the data decides whether A is worth it.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: measure first (B) vs optimize on a guess (A) vs a cache that is wrong across workers and restarts (C).

options.label: Recompute per attempt + per-attempt timing metric, revisit with data (recommended)
options.description:
✅ No new correctness surface; retries stay stateless and identical to attempt 1
✅ Metric (payload fetch ms, graph build ms, per attempt) gives the evidence to justify caching later (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~5 min)
❌ Heavy jobs pay the full fetch + rebuild up to 5 times if they keep failing

options.label: Persist the computed graph on the job record at attempt 1
options.description:
✅ Attempts 2..N skip the payload iteration entirely
✅ Survives restarts and works across workers because it lives on the job record (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min)
❌ Needs a payload version/hash to invalidate; schema change on the job record; optimizes an unmeasured cost

options.label: In-process memoization keyed by job id
options.description:
✅ Smallest code change; no schema touch
✅ Helps when the same worker process retries the same job (human: ~2 hr / CC: ~5 min)
❌ Lost on restart and wrong when another worker picks up the retry; unbounded memory if not evicted

answers.D9 \u2014 Cache the dependency graph acr: Recompute per attempt + per-attempt timing metric, revisit with data (recommended)

D11 — TODO: move webhooks to at-least-once delivery with an idempotency key header?

The plan copies those steps into each of 5 workers and also re-implements the scheduler the job library already has (PLAN.md:6-8 admits it is the "same shape"). The question is whether the retry machinery is the library's job with your curve plugged in, one shared helper you own, or five hand copies.
Stakes if we pick wrong: five copies means a jitter or logging fix lands in five places and drifts; owning the scheduler means owning attempt persistence, requeue, and crash-mid-retry semantics the library already handles.
Recommendation: A because you keep the curve (the thing you said you want) and give up only the plumbing you did not want to own. [Layer 1]
Completeness: A=10/10, B=8/10, C=3/10
Net: control over the curve is cheap in all three; control over scheduling is expensive and only C and B pay for it.

options.label: Library retry hook + one custom backoff() (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Attempt counting, requeue, and crash-safety stay in battle-tested library code (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
✅ The curve is one pure function in one file, trivially unit-testable with a table of (attempt -> delay)
❌ Curve shape is bounded by what the hook's signature lets you return (delay ms per attempt); verify it accepts a function

options.label: One shared withRetry() module, custom scheduler
options.description:
✅ Full ownership of scheduling and curve, still exactly one implementation for all 5 workers (human: ~3 days / CC: ~45 min)
✅ Works even if the library hook turns out not to accept a custom function
❌ You now own attempt persistence and what happens when a worker dies between failure and re-dispatch

options.label: Keep inline copies in 5 workers (as written)
options.description:
✅ No shared abstraction to design; each worker is self-contained (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min)
✅ Zero coordination between worker owners while landing
❌ Five copies of the same body; any bug or log-field change must be found and fixed five times

answers.D4 \u2014 R1: Where should the retry env: Library retry hook + one custom backoff() (recommended)

questions.question:
D5 — R2: Add jitter to the backoff curve?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md retry framework, `backoff()` function approved in D4.
ELI10: If 500 jobs fail together when a downstream API blips, a plain exponential curve makes all 500 retry at exactly the same second, then again at 2s, 4s, 8s. That synchronized wave ("thundering herd") can knock the API over again. Jitter multiplies each delay by a random factor so the retries spread out. PLAN.md mentions no jitter.
Stakes if we pick wrong: without jitter, a recovering dependency gets hit by the full retry wave at once and the outage repeats on a schedule; with jitter, individual retry timing becomes non-deterministic (tests must inject the RNG).
Recommendation: A because full jitter is the documented industry default (AWS, resilience4j) and costs one injected random() call.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10
Net: one seeded random call versus a retry storm that recreates the incident you are retrying from.

options.label: Full jitter: random() * min(cap, base * 2^attempt) (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Spreads a batch of simultaneous failures across the whole delay window, protecting the recovering dependency
✅ Still one pure function; tests pass a fixed RNG and assert the bounds (human: ~2h / CC: ~5 min)
❌ Individual job wait time is no longer predictable from the attempt number alone

options.label: Deterministic exponential (no jitter)
options.description:
✅ Exact delay per attempt is readable from a table; simplest to reason about in logs
✅ No RNG to inject or seed in tests
❌ Correlated failures retry in lockstep and can re-trigger the outage they are recovering from

questions.question:
D6 — R3: Cap the per-attempt delay?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md retry framework; curve = full jitter over base * 2^attempt (D5).
ELI10: Doubling with no ceiling grows fast: with a 1-second base, attempt 10 waits ~17 minutes, attempt 15 waits ~9 hours, attempt 20 waits ~12 days. A cap says "never wait more than X between tries", so a job that finally can succeed is not parked for hours. PLAN.md names no cap.
Stakes if we pick wrong: uncapped, a job past attempt ~12 is effectively stuck for hours while the dependency has long recovered; too low a cap hammers a dependency that is down for a while (mitigated by max attempts, R4).
Recommendation: A because a 5-minute ceiling with 1 s base is the conventional shape and per-worker override keeps "full control" where a worker needs a different curve.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=4/10
Net: one `min()` and two named constants versus jobs silently parked for hours.

options.label: Cap at 5 min, base 1 s, per-worker override (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Worst-case wait between attempts is bounded and readable in one config constant (300,000 ms)
✅ Per-worker override preserves the curve control the plan asked for without forking the function
❌ A dependency down for 30+ minutes gets probed every ~5 min until max attempts is hit

options.label: No cap (pure exponential)
options.description:
✅ Simplest formula, one fewer constant to document
✅ Backs off very aggressively from a dependency that is hard-down
❌ By attempt 15 a job waits ~9 hours; recovery of the dependency does not shorten the wait

answers.D6 \u2014 R3: Cap the per-attempt delay?: Cap at 5 min, base 1 s, per-worker override (recommended)

questions.question:
D7 — R4: When do retries stop, and where does the job go?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md retry framework; curve now jittered and capped (D5, D6).
ELI10: A retry loop needs an exit. "Max attempts" says how many tries before giving up; the terminal disposition says what happens to the job then: parked in a dead-letter/failed queue an operator can inspect and replay, or simply dropped. PLAN.md specifies neither, so as written a job could retry forever or vanish.
Stakes if we pick wrong: unbounded means a poison job (bad payload) burns a worker slot every 5 minutes indefinitely; drop-only means a customer's webhook silently never arrives and nobody can replay it at 3am.
Recommendation: A because the library already has a failed/dead-letter state and 8 attempts with the D6 curve is roughly 25 minutes of coverage, enough for a typical dependency blip.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=2/10
Net: an inspectable parking lot for exhausted jobs versus either silent loss or an infinite loop.

options.label: 8 attempts, then dead-letter + terminal log (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Exhausted jobs are inspectable and replayable from the library's failed set; nothing is lost silently (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
✅ Terminal log line carries job id, attempt count, last error, so alerting can key on it
❌ Dead-letter set needs an owner and a retention policy or it grows unbounded

options.label: 8 attempts, then drop with a log line
options.description:
✅ No dead-letter storage to manage or clean up
✅ Still bounds worker time spent on poison jobs
❌ The job is gone; a customer-facing webhook that exhausts retries cannot be replayed

options.label: Unbounded retries
options.description:
✅ Never gives up on a job that will eventually succeed
✅ No max-attempts constant to tune per worker
❌ A malformed payload retries every 5 minutes forever, holding a worker slot and spamming logs

questions.question:
D8 — R5: Retry every error, or only transient ones?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md retry framework; exhaustion goes to dead-letter after 8 (D7).
ELI10: Some failures fix themselves if you wait (a timeout, a 503, a dropped connection). Others never will (a 400 because the payload is malformed, a validation error, a serialization bug). PLAN.md retries everything the same way, so a permanently broken job spends ~25 minutes and 8 attempts before anyone sees it, and every attempt re-fetches the payload (the Performance section's cost).
Stakes if we pick wrong: retrying permanent errors wastes worker capacity and delays the dead-letter signal by 25 minutes; classifying wrong (marking a transient error permanent) sends a recoverable job to dead-letter on its first try.
Recommendation: A because the classification is a small predicate with a conservative default (unknown error = retryable), so the failure mode of a wrong guess is the current behavior, not lost jobs.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Net: one `isRetryable(err)` predicate versus 8x the work and a 25-minute delay on every permanently broken job.

options.label: Classify: retry transient, dead-letter permanent (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Malformed payloads reach the dead-letter set on attempt 1 instead of attempt 8, 25 min sooner (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
✅ Unknown errors default to retryable, so a missed classification degrades to today's behavior, never to loss
❌ One more predicate to maintain as new error types appear from dependencies

options.label: Retry every error until max attempts
options.description:
✅ No classification predicate; every failure follows one path
✅ Impossible to wrongly fast-fail a transient error
❌ A 400 from a bad payload costs 8 attempts, 8 payload re-fetches, and ~25 minutes before it surfaces

questions.question:
D9 — R6: What delivery guarantee does processWebhookJob() have after retries?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md:16-18 rewrites `processWebhookJob()`, today at-most-once.
ELI10: At-most-once means a webhook is sent once or not at all; receivers never see duplicates. Retrying a send that timed out can deliver it twice if the receiver actually got the first one. So "add retries" quietly changes the promise to at-least-once. The honest options: keep the promise by exempting webhooks, or change it deliberately and give receivers a stable id so they can drop duplicates.
Stakes if we pick wrong: undeclared duplicates mean a receiver charges a card or sends an email twice; exempting webhooks means transient failures keep dropping deliveries, which is the pain this plan exists to fix.
Recommendation: A because it is the standard webhook contract (Stripe, GitHub) and the delivered-marker check keeps duplicates rare rather than merely tolerable.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=5/10
Net: a header and one marker row versus either silent double-processing at receivers or leaving webhooks as the one flow that still drops on a blip.

options.label: At-least-once + idempotency key + delivered marker (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Receivers get a stable per-job id header and can dedupe; matches how major webhook providers behave (human: ~1.5 days / CC: ~30 min)
✅ Persisted delivered marker checked before each attempt means a timed-out-but-received send is not re-sent after the marker lands
❌ Contract change for receivers must be documented; a receiver that ignores the header can still see a duplicate in the timeout window

options.label: At-least-once, no idempotency key
options.description:
✅ Smallest change: webhooks simply join the retry framework like the other 4 workers
✅ No new header or marker storage
❌ Receivers have no way to detect duplicates; a timeout on a processed request causes a real double side effect

options.label: Keep at-most-once: exempt webhooks from retries
options.description:
✅ Existing receiver contract is untouched; zero duplicate risk
✅ Regression test is simple: assert exactly one send attempt ever
❌ Webhooks stay fire-and-forget; a 2-second dependency blip still loses the delivery for good

questions.question:
D10 — R7: How do we protect processWebhookJob() behavior through the rewrite?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md:16-18 rewrite; new contract per D9 (at-least-once + idempotency key + marker).
ELI10: The webhook sender is being rewritten and its promise is changing on purpose. A regression test pins down what must NOT change (one 2xx send per success, request body and signature byte-identical to today) and what changes deliberately (retries, the new header). The question is only how deep the proof goes: drive a fake HTTP receiver end to end, or mock the HTTP client in a unit test.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a mock-only test cannot catch the timeout-then-2xx double-send or a marker written before the send actually completes; those are exactly the bugs this rewrite can introduce.
Recommendation: A because the failure modes live at the HTTP and persistence boundary, where mocks hide them, and a fake receiver is ~40 lines. [→E2E]
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10
Net: a small fake receiver versus trusting that mocks model a timeout the same way a socket does.

options.label: Integration suite vs fake receiver, 5 cases + golden fixture (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Exercises real timeout, real marker persistence, and byte-identical body/signature vs a golden fixture (human: ~1.5 days / CC: ~30 min)
✅ Covers timeout-then-2xx and ack-lost cases, the two ways the rewrite can double-send
❌ Needs a local fake receiver and a persistence fixture in CI; slower than unit tests

options.label: Unit test with mocked HTTP client, 3 cases
options.description:
✅ Fast, no network or fixture setup; runs in the normal unit suite (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
✅ Pins send count and header on success, timeout-then-2xx, and 4xx paths
❌ A mock cannot reproduce a socket timeout after the receiver processed the request, so the ack-lost double-send is untested

answers.D10 \u2014 R7: How do we protect process: Integration suite vs fake receiver, 5 cases + golden fixture (recommended)

questions.question:
D11 — R9: Cache the dependency graph across retry attempts?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md:21-24; retries now capped at 8 attempts (D7).
ELI10: Each attempt currently reloads the whole job payload from the database and rebuilds a dependency graph from it, even though the payload has not changed since attempt 1. Caching means: build the graph once, store the result next to the job, and let attempts 2-8 read it back. The plan calls this out and then says "not planned".
Stakes if we pick wrong: leaving it means retries multiply DB load exactly when the system is already unhealthy (a retry storm is 500 extra reads per wave); caching wrong means a stale graph if the payload is edited between attempts, hence the version check.
Recommendation: A because the plan already identified the fix, the cost is a serialize/deserialize pair and one version field, and the win lands where load is worst.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=3/10
Net: one persisted field with a version guard versus retry load that grows with the number of attempts.

options.label: Cache graph on the job record, version-guarded (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Attempts 2-8 skip the payload read and graph build; retry storms stop multiplying DB reads (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
✅ Version guard (payload hash or updated_at) invalidates the cache if the payload changes between attempts
❌ Serialized graph adds bytes to each job record; needs a size sanity check for very large payloads

options.label: Instrument first, decide in a follow-up
options.description:
✅ Decision gets made on measured payload size and graph build time instead of a guess
✅ Metrics are useful regardless of the eventual choice
❌ Ships the framework with the known 8x cost intact; the follow-up needs an owner or it becomes the plan's 'later'

options.label: Recompute every attempt (as written)
options.description:
✅ No new persisted field, no invalidation logic, simplest code
✅ Always operates on the freshest payload
❌ Every retry pays the full read + build cost, and it lands during the outage that caused the retries

answers.D11 \u2014 R9: Cache the dependency grap: Cache graph on the job record, version-guarded (recommended)

questions.question:
D12 — TODO: Dead-letter set retention, owner, and alert
Project/branch/task: `main`, follows from D7 (exhausted jobs park in the library's failed set).
ELI10: D7 gives exhausted jobs a parking lot. A parking lot with no attendant fills up and nobody notices the cars. This TODO is the attendant: an alert when the failed set grows, a retention window (e.g. purge after 30 days), and a named owner.
What: Alert on dead-letter growth, define retention, assign an owner. Why: without it the failed set grows unbounded and exhausted webhooks sit unnoticed. Context: D7 terminal log carries jobId/attempts/lastError; alert can key on that log line or on library failed-set size; start in the ops/alerting config. Effort: S. Priority: P2. Depends on: D7 landing.
Stakes if we pick wrong: skipping means the first sign of a dead-letter pileup is a customer asking where their webhook went.
Recommendation: A because it is a follow-up to an approved behavior, not part of the retry framework itself.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: capture the ops follow-up now versus rediscovering it during an incident.

options.label: Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
options.description:
✅ The ops half of D7 is captured with context while the reasoning is fresh
✅ Keeps this PR scoped to the framework; alerting lands in its own change
❌ TODOS.md must be created after plan mode exits; one more file in the repo

options.label: Skip: not valuable enough
options.description:
✅ No new file or backlog entry
✅ Team may already have generic queue alerting that covers this
❌ If no such alerting exists, dead-letter growth is invisible until a customer reports it

options.label: Build it now in this PR
options.description:
✅ Framework ships with its alert; nothing to forget
✅ Retention and alert are ~30 lines of config
❌ Widens this PR into ops/alerting config, a different review surface (human: +half day / CC: +10 min)

questions.question:
D13 — TODO: Close the check-then-send race on webhook delivery
Project/branch/task: `main`, residual from D9 (marker checked before each send).
ELI10: D9 checks "already delivered?" then sends. If the job library hands the same job to two workers at once (it can, on redelivery after a worker crash), both can pass the check before either writes the marker, so the receiver gets two sends despite the marker. The Idempotency-Key lets the receiver drop the duplicate, so this is rare and tolerable, not silent loss. Closing it fully needs a lease: claim the marker row before sending, not after.
What: Replace check-then-send with claim-then-send (insert marker row in `pending` state first, unique on job id). Why: removes the last duplicate-send window; receivers without dedup logic stop seeing doubles. Context: D9 marker table exists; add a `state` column (pending/delivered) and a unique constraint; start in `processWebhookJob`. Effort: M. Priority: P3. Depends on: D9 landing.
Stakes if we pick wrong: skipping leaves a rare duplicate window that the header already mitigates; building now adds a state machine to a PR that is already changing the delivery contract.
Recommendation: A because the header covers the residual for now and the lease deserves its own focused change.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: document a known rare window versus growing this PR by a state machine.

options.label: Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
options.description:
✅ The residual race is written down with the exact fix, not lost in a review transcript
✅ This PR stays focused on the retry framework plus the D9 contract
❌ Duplicates in the redelivery window remain possible until the follow-up lands

options.label: Skip: not valuable enough
options.description:
✅ Idempotency-Key already gives receivers a dedupe handle; many will never notice
✅ No backlog entry to maintain
❌ Receivers that ignore the header can still double-process on a worker crash

options.label: Build it now in this PR
options.description:
✅ Delivery contract lands fully closed in one change; no residual to document
✅ Unique constraint + state column is a small migration (human: +1 day / CC: +20 min)
❌ Adds a migration and a pending/delivered state machine to a PR already changing delivery semantics

questions.question:
D14 — What next?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md retry framework; eng review CLEAR, 10 tasks, 0 unresolved.
